source.title: Mixture of Wide Experts: Sparse Routing for Interpretable Native Coordinates
source.authors: Tavish Mankash; Vardhaman Kalloli; Keshava Prasad; Deepan Muthirayan

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses TopK SAEs as a post-hoc interpretability comparison and reports reconstruction diagnostics, but it does not test whether SAE error is linearly predictable, how error norms behave across SAE sizes, or whether SAE error affects model computation as the claim versions specify.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation fraction of variance unexplained and dead-feature fractions for site-matched TopK SAEs. These are direct SAE reconstruction diagnostics, so they are recorded below, but the paper does not analyze the structure or function of the reconstruction error. Interpretability scores, steering effects, and cited SAE results do not test the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper introduces an architecture (MoWE) and uses site-matched TopK SAEs only as a readability baseline. It reports SAE validation FVU and dead-feature fractions (Table 19), but never analyses whether SAE error is linearly predictable, how it scales across SAE sizes, whether splicing it in harms loss beyond random error, or whether circuits or steering lose behaviour without it. Its case studies steer native coordinates, not SAE features. The error-magnitude diagnostics are a related but different construct (overall reconstruction quality across architectures) and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that write-disjoint routing (MoWE) makes native FFN-update coordinates more specific and readable than dense or standard MoE, comparable to a dense TopK SAE. SAEs remain complementary for finer decomposition. The FVU values are reported only as diagnostics; the authors draw no conclusion about SAE error structure or function.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains TopK SAEs on FFN updates to compare feature readability and reports FVU and dead-feature diagnostics. It does not apply a method for analyzing dark-matter predictability, scaling, or functional effects.

fits_no_version.finding: The same TopK SAE configuration (12,288 features, k=38) yields much lower validation FVU on MoWE FFN updates (0.00277) than on dense FFN updates (0.0622), with higher dead-feature fractions (0.701 vs 0.524).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE reconstruction error at a fixed SAE configuration depends on the host model's architecture: write-disjoint routed FFN outputs are far easier to reconstruct than dense FFN outputs.

record.problems: The all-layer interpretability study uses one checkpoint per architecture; only live SAE features are evaluated for readability, with mean dead-feature fractions of 0.524 for dense and 0.701 for MoWE. The SAE diagnostics are not used to test the dark-matter claim versions.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were left out. The paper's SAE feature-specificity scores and post-block SAE comparisons assess readability rather than the structure or function of reconstruction error.

untested.parts: All: whether SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.
All: error-norm predictability across SAE sizes, same-context failure, and persistence with scale. Only one SAE size (12,288 features) is trained.
All: no spliced-in loss comparison against random errors.
All: no decomposition of the error into a linear and a nonlinear part.
All: no SAE-feature circuit or steering analysis with or without the error term.
All: SAE architecture and objective are not varied, and the error is not attributed to training choices versus representation structure.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is correct. The post-block TopK and L1 SAEs (Table 20) report only readability, not error, so there is nothing further to record. None of the case-study steering uses SAE features, so V5 is untouched.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a large share of SAE error is a linear function of the input activation.
Whether per-token error norms are predictable across SAE sizes, whether larger SAEs fail on the same contexts, or whether error persists with scale.
Whether replacing activations with SAE reconstructions harms model loss more than random errors of the same size.
Whether linear error reflects unlearned features and nonlinear error is qualitatively different or resists further dictionary learning.
Whether analyses of SAE features lose model behavior unless the SAE error term is retained.

The paper reports dead-feature fractions but does not test whether SAE training choices cause dark matter, whether alternative architectures or end-to-end training reduce it, or whether error reflects representation structure.

relation.reason: The study discusses SAE decomposition and its limitations and reports reconstruction diagnostics, without testing or using a dark-matter claim.

tranche.reason: The study compares native-coordinate readability and SAE features. Reconstruction and dead-feature diagnostics do not test error predictability, SAE-size scaling, functional consequences of reconstruction error, or its attribution to SAE training.

source_check.notes: The authors-conclusion paraphrase is accurate. Diagnostics average 19 layers from one checkpoint per architecture; readability evaluation includes only live SAE features. The architecture comparison does not isolate SAE-training causes under V6.
